title: When you miss a day
tomorrow: a Thursday sit full of strangers. why would Mai go?

segments.voice: Yesterday was your evening: the day put down, its good given away. That finished a whole day of practice, morning to night. Now the harder question: what happens when a day goes missing?
screen: `THE DAY PUT DOWN.` → `AND WHEN A DAY GOES MISSING?`

segments.voice: Mai's first two days at the program: a bus, a key card, a roommate, a studio at seven. She didn't sit once. Now it's night three, and the thought arrives: ruined already. A monk in the old stories stood with the same thought at a gate. His name was Cula Panthaka. For months he'd tried to learn a single verse, and every new line pushed out the one before it. His own brother, a respected monk, told him to go home. So he stood outside the monastery gate, crying. Then someone came out.
screen: `TWO DAYS, NO SITTING.` → `RUINED ALREADY?` → `A MONK CRYING AT THE GATE.` → `SOMEONE COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: It was the Buddha. In Cula Panthaka's own verses, in the Theragatha, the Teacher touches his head, takes him by the arm, leads him back inside, and hands him a clean cloth. The commentary fills in the rest. Sit in the sun, the Buddha says, rub this cloth, and repeat: removing dirt. As he rubs, the white cloth turns gray from his hands. Watching it change, he understands: the mind gathers dust the same way, and it's cleaned the same way, one rub at a time. The commentary says he was awakened before the day was out. The Dhammapada verse told with his story says it in Max Müller's words: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm." An island isn't made in one day. It's made by coming back. That's the teaching under the story. Practice isn't a streak to protect. It's a cloth you pick up again. Notice what the Buddha didn't do at the gate: no scolding, no count of the months lost. He gave the man a next step. Two missed days don't erase a seat, a morning or three reminders. They only mean tonight is the night for the next rub.
screen: `THE BUDDHA LEADS HIM BACK IN.` · `A CLEAN CLOTH: REMOVING DIRT.` · `AN ISLAND, MADE BY COMING BACK.` · `NO SCOLDING. A NEXT STEP.` · then, large: `BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Take hold of any cloth within reach: a sleeve, a scarf, the hem of your shirt. Rub it slowly between your fingers, and with each breath, quietly begin again. When the mind wanders, that isn't failure; it's the next rub.
When you miss a day: not a broken streak, but the moment to pick up the cloth again.
screen: `WHEN YOU MISS A DAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: begin again. The Buddha gave the man at the gate a cloth, not a lecture. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1730 COUNTS.` → `DAILY PRACTICE · 5 OF 5.` → `TOMORROW: A ROOM FULL OF STRANGERS. WHY GO?`

howItsDone: In Buddhist teaching a lapse in practice is met the way a wandering mind is met in meditation: you notice you have stopped, and you start again, without blame.

fork.setup: a friend who keeps a daily Buddhist sit missed a week while sick. she says she'll restart on the first of the month, 'so it's clean.' what fits the story?

wait for the new month so the record looks clean

fork.reveal: the Buddha didn't wait for a clean start: he handed Cula Panthaka a cloth that same day. begin again is the whole instruction.

chat.says: day 3 here. didn't sit once, bus then orientation. i literally just started. is it already ruined?
options: not ruined. the Buddha met a monk who'd failed for months and gave him a cloth: begin again.
kind of. a practice is a streak, so restart from zero and promise not to miss again.
skip it till you're home; six weeks away is a break from practice anyway.
chat.meaning: Cula Panthaka failed for months; the Buddha didn't scold him but gave him a cloth to rub. Practice is begun again, not guarded like a streak.

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

notes: Cula Panthaka: in his Theragatha verses he is slow, his brother (Maha Panthaka) drives him out, he stands grieving at the gate, and the Teacher touches his head, leads him in by the arm and gives him a cloth. The commentary (Dhammapada commentary on v.25, also the Anguttara commentary) adds the months spent on one verse, rubbing the cloth in the sun while repeating 'removing dirt', the cloth turning soiled, and his awakening that day.
